JUDAISM - THE WAY OF THE TORAH - STUDY NOTES

THE SHEMA (DEUTERONOMY 6:4-9)
- 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord alone. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.'
- Keep these words in your heart, teach them to your children, talk about them at home and away, bind them on your hand, fix them on your forehead, write them on doorposts and gates.

WHY JUDAISM IS REMARKABLE
- Monotheistic faith: belief in one God. Judaism is the world's oldest monotheistic faith - the first great religion to say there is only one God, against the polytheism of the time.
- It is the 'parent' of Christianity and Islam.
- Religious practice goes beyond ceremonies to how we treat others: 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18).
- Torah: the law of God in the first five books of the Bible. Its centrepiece is the Ten Commandments, the foundation of many legal codes.
- Pious Jews show love of God by obeying the Torah.
- Jews believe they are chosen by God for a special relationship and a special role - to bring all people to know the one God. Isaiah 2:3: 'For out of Zion shall go forth instruction, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.'
- God is creator of everything; everything depends on God. God is personal: 'the God of Abraham, the God of Jacob, the God of Israel' (Exodus 3:6), a God of love and justice.
- The world has a purpose: to build a kingdom of love, peace and freedom. All life has meaning.
- 'The people of the Book': because of their emphasis on studying sacred texts. Talmud: 'Learning God's teaching is equal to everything else.'
- Gamaliel: 'Excellent is the study of the Torah combined with a worldly occupation, for the toil involved on both sides makes sin to be forgotten.'
- Despite persecution, exile, enslavement and bigotry, Jews have kept their faith and passed it on.
- Though small in number, Jews have greatly influenced culture, business and intellectual thought.

ORIGINS
- Jewish history goes back nearly four thousand years to the Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 12-27).
- Recorded in what Jews call the Holy Writings and Christians call the Old Testament.
- Covenant: a sacred agreement/alliance between God and the people; a relationship of total commitment of one side to the other.
- First covenant made through Abraham; renewed by Isaac, Jacob, and by Moses after about four hundred years of slavery in Egypt.

VISION OF SALVATION
- Moses Maimonides (1135-1204): 'I believe with all my heart, that God who made the world... is the maker and the guide of every creature.'
- Central value: reverence for and holiness of all life. Humans are made in God's image, so human life is sacred.
- Every area of life, from the exalted to the mundane, has value. Jewish law covers working, eating, dressing, relationships and nature.
- Focus: to hallow all of life and work for justice, righteousness and freedom.
- Separating the spiritual journey from daily tasks is contrary to Jewish thought. Work of mind and hands is praise to God (Proverbs 18:9).
- Speculation about the afterlife is of little importance; God judges how one lives here and now.
- Wisdom 3:1-9: 'the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them... they are at peace... their hope is full of immortality.'
- This belief never addresses resurrection or a soul without a body. Life after death, though not clear in Hebrew scriptures, has been a fundamental belief for two thousand years. Many Jews see the scriptures as symbolic and trust in God's mercy.
- Yahweh: the creator God who speaks to the Jewish people; the God of the Covenant.
- Covenant first with Abraham, reaffirmed at Mount Sinai, renewed through the Prophets - an experience of God's grace and God's demands.
- Teshuvah: repentance - even sinners can repent and return to the merciful God.
- High Holy Days, especially the Day of Atonement: look back on sins, regret them, commit never to repeat them.
- Rabbi Sir Immanuel Jakobovits: 'We are primarily a social religion. We always use the word salvation in a collective sense, never in an individual sense. And the emphasis is on deed, not creed. Pure faith is meaningless unless translated into behaviour... we are accountable to God.'
- So all of life is governed by laws (worship, business, diet). No distinction between religious and secular. All of life is a daily blessing.
- Mitzvot: the commandments of God. Jews are free to accept or reject them; responding with obedient love and loyalty is accepting God's offer of salvation. This brings deep joy.

A COMMUNITY OF BELIEVERS
- Community is central. First experienced in the home, then in festivals and Sabbath ceremonies.
- Most Jews belong to a local synagogue led by a rabbi.
- The rabbi is elected by the congregation and accountable to them. His authority is based on learning and study, not on mediating God's love and forgiveness. He may be spokesperson for the community, but that is the limit of his authority.
- Sabbath (Shabbat): the weekly day of rest focusing on God the creator, who rested on the seventh day.
- Enjoyment of good things and joy in God's presence are central. Resting from work, company and the Sabbath meal build community and identity.
- Psalm 104:15: praise God for 'wine to gladden the human heart, oil to make the face shine, and bread to strengthen the human heart'.
- The Sabbath is a reminder of dependence on God and a memorial of creation; a time of retreat, worship, prayer and family.
- Greeting: 'Shabbat Shalom' - 'peaceful Sabbath'.
- In the synagogue the climax is opening the Ark of the Covenant (a cupboard facing Jerusalem) and carrying the Torah scroll around; bells tinkle and people touch it with the fringes of their prayer shawls (talliths).
- Tallith: prayer shawl.

A CELEBRATING TRADITION
- Lunar calendar; many festivals came from agricultural seasons and historical events.
- Three major festivals: Passover (Pesach), Pentecost (Shavuot), Tabernacles (Sukkot).
- Less important: Festival of Lights (Hanukkah), Festival of Lots (Purim).
- Most important: the two high holy days - Rosh Hashanah (New Year) and Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement).
- Jewish calendar runs in cycles of nineteen years, inserting extra months to keep seasons right.
- Pilgrimage: biblical command for every male to go to the Temple three times a year on the Three Foot festivals (Passover, Shavuot, Succot).
- Western (Wailing) Wall in Jerusalem: all that remains of the Temple, destroyed in 70 CE - key focus of pilgrimage.
- Masada: fortress on the western side of the Dead Sea where the Zealots held out against the Romans in 70 CE; their heroism inspires all Jews.

FESTIVALS - GROUPS
- Biblical (major): the three foot festivals, New Year and Day of Atonement.
- Later (minor): Hanukkah, Purim, Fast of Tisha b'Av.
- Modern: Israel's Independence Day, Holocaust Memorial Day, Jerusalem Day.

AUTUMN
- Rosh Hashanah ('head of the year'), also the Day of Blowing: celebrates the birth of the world and the annual judgement of mankind. Prayer and reflection. Apple dipped in honey for a sweet year. Greeting: 'May you be written for a good year ahead'. Shofar (ram's horn) blown to call people to the ways of God.
- Ten Days of Penitence: self-examination and prayers for forgiveness.
- Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement): 24-hour fast; services all day; public confession of sin; white robes for purity and the grave (the dead are buried in white). Purely religious - no historical significance.
- Succot (Tabernacles): Festival of Ingathering of the harvest; a foot festival. Thanks for God's care during forty years in the desert. Temporary shelters with roofs of branches and leaves so the stars are visible; meals eaten there.
- Simchat Torah (Rejoicing of the Law): end of Succot; one day; celebrates finishing the yearly reading of the Torah and starting again. Scrolls carried in procession with singing and dancing. Last chapter of Deuteronomy and first chapter of Genesis read.

WINTER
- Hanukkah (Festival of Dedication): eight days; victory over the Syrians and Greeks who desecrated the Temple and brought paganism. Candles lit each night, one more each night until all eight. Foods cooked in oil recall the miracle of one day's oil lasting eight days. Money given to children.
- Purim (Festival of Lots): one day; recalls Queen Esther who saved her people from Haman of Persia, who cast lots to decide when to destroy the Jews. Book of Esther read; noises of derision at Haman's name; fancy dress and carnivals.

SPRING
- Passover (Pesach), Feast of Unleavened Bread: a foot festival; eight days; celebrates deliverance from Egypt. Seder: special home meal where the Haggadah (story of the Exodus) is read; children take an active part ('Why is this night different from all other nights?'). Most important symbolic food: Matzah (unleavened bread).

SUMMER
- Shavuot (Pentecost, Feast of Weeks): fifty days after Passover; a foot festival. Celebrates the giving of the Law (Ten Commandments) to Moses on Mount Sinai. Some stay up all night studying. Also Feast of the First Fruits: synagogue decorated with flowers; dairy foods eaten.
- Ninth of Av (Tisha b'Av): day of mourning and fasting ending three weeks of mourning for the destruction of the Temples (586 BCE and 70 CE). Ornaments removed, lights dimmed, Book of Lamentations read.

MODERN FESTIVALS
- Holocaust Memorial Day (Yom HaShoah): on the anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto uprising (1943), shortly after Passover.
- Israel Independence Day (Yom HaAtzmaut): 5 Iyar, late April or early May.
- Jerusalem Day (Yom Yerushalayim): before Shavuot; reunification of Jerusalem in the Six Day War, 1967.
- All festivals follow the Hebrew calendar, so dates vary on the secular calendar.

RITES OF PASSAGE
- Brit Milah: circumcision of boys at eight days old (Genesis 17:11-12); symbol of the Covenant between Abraham and God. Done by a trained Mohel, with prayers and blessings; the child is named.
- Girls are named in the synagogue on the first day of Torah reading after birth.
- Bar Mitzvah ('son of the law'): boy at thirteen; becomes a responsible member. Can be counted in the Minyan (quorum of ten men for a full service), help lead services and read Torah. Fasts on Yom Kippur, keeps all commandments, is responsible for his actions. Wears tefillin.
- Tefillin (phylacteries): leather boxes containing Torah passages, worn on forehead and arm in weekday morning prayer.
- Before Bar Mitzvah a boy studies Hebrew, scripture and prayer. He does not touch the Torah page with his hand, out of reverence.
- Bat Mitzvah ('daughter of the commandment'): girl at twelve; must keep the commandments and is responsible for her actions. Does not lead services in Orthodox synagogues. Public celebration is a modern custom.
- Marriage: no tradition of celibacy; marriage is God's intention (Genesis 2:24; 9:1-7). Three elements: a) Ketuba - marriage document; b) Chuppah - wedding canopy representing their new home; c) Living together.
- Groom places a ring on the bride: 'Behold thou art consecrated to me with this ring according to the laws of Moses and Israel'. Seven blessings recited. A glass is broken to remember the destruction of the Temple - while it does not stand, a Jew cannot enjoy total happiness. Couple spend time alone, then a festive meal; seven blessings again; sips of wine.
- Divorce permitted if the marriage has irretrievably broken down: a Get (divorce document) prepared by a Bet Din (three rabbis), handed by husband to wife. Ketuba and Get are handwritten and witnessed.
- Death: family arranges the funeral; Chevra Kadisha ('holy group') volunteers help. Burial within twenty-four hours. Onen: close family between death and burial.
- Shiva ('seven'): seven days of intense mourning at home; low stools, mirrors covered, torn garment worn, candle lit, prayers including the Kaddish; neighbours bring food.
- Kaddish recited for nearly a year at daily services.
- Sheloshim: first thirty days; ends mourning for sibling, spouse or child. For a parent, Avelut (mourning) lasts a year.
- Gravestone erected after a year. On each anniversary a candle is lit and Kaddish recited.

CHALLENGES TO THE TRADITION
- Modern state of Israel established 1948 - the Promised Land. Faith can be lived there without fear of persecution. The link has religious, political, historical and psychological dimensions.
- David Ben Gurion, first prime minister of Israel: suffering in the Diaspora drove immigration, but it was the 'Messianic vision' that guided it to the creation of the State. 'The ingathering of the exiles... is the beginning of the realisation of the Messianic vision.'
- Diaspora: Jews living outside Israel.
- Disagreement over land: all promised to Abraham, or less for peace. Rifts between the religious zeal of Zionism and those willing to negotiate.
- Jewish-Islamic relations strained by Middle East tensions despite a shared monotheism and prophets.
- Rise of secular Jews: can the community accept those linked by identity rather than faith?
- Ultra-Orthodox Hasidic Jews: minority, mainly Jerusalem, speak Yiddish, distinctive dress and hair.
- Non-Orthodox: Conservative, Liberal, Progressive, Reform - different rules on diet, scripture and women's role. Conservative Judaism preserves essential traditions in a modern world.
- About 18 million Jews worldwide - 40 per cent in the USA, 20 per cent in Israel.

CHRISTIANITY AND JUDAISM (HIGHER LEVEL)
- Shared scripture: Hebrew Bible / Old Testament; belief in one creator and the dignity of people made in God's image.
- Greatest gift of Judaism to Christianity: Jesus himself. To understand Jesus, Christians must appreciate his Jewishness.
- Both see love of God and neighbour as inseparable; both stress the holiness of creation.
- Most of the first Christians were Jewish; their worship, prayer and organisation were the foundation of Church practice.
- Psalms and prophets treasured by both. Fixed times of daily prayer have Jewish roots.
- Hebrew words in Christian use: Messiah, Amen, Alleluia.
- Council of Christians and Jews: fosters dialogue.
- Anti-Semitism: hostility to Jews; centuries of it, often initiated or ignored by the Church, left deep hurt.
- Pope John Paul II called Jews 'our beloved elder brothers' and asked forgiveness. At Yad Vashem (2000): 'We wish to remember... to ensure that never again will evil prevail'.
- Pope Pius XI: 'We are all spiritually Semites.' Pope John XXIII (1960): 'I am Joseph, your brother.'
- German Bishops (1980): anti-Semitism is ultimately against Christ himself.
- Sisters of Sion: religious order working for Jewish-Christian reconciliation.

THE IRISH JEWISH COMMUNITY
- First reference: Annals of Inishfallen, 1079 - 'five Jews came over the sea' to the king and 'were sent back again'.
- A few came in the 12th and 14th centuries; then Sephardic Jews (from Spain and Portugal) after expulsions in the late 15th/early 16th centuries; records from the 1500s.
- Dublin community from the 1600s; Cork and Dublin cemeteries early 1700s; Belfast from the mid 1700s.
- Late 19th century anti-Semitism in Eastern Europe brought many Jews. Communities in Derry, Lurgan, Limerick, Cork, Waterford, but mostly Dublin - north of the Liffey, then Dolphin's Barn and Portobello: 'Little Jerusalem'. Shops in Lower Clanbrassil Street.
- From 1946 Jews moved to the south suburbs; many synagogues closed.
- Walworth Road synagogue (1917) became the Irish Jewish Museum, opened in June 1985 by Chaim Herzog, Irish-born President of Israel, whose father had been Chief Rabbi of the Irish Free State.
- Population: under 1,200 today, from a peak of 5,400 in 1945.
- Ettie (Esther) Steinberg: Irish citizen married in Greenville Synagogue, Terenure, 1937; died at Auschwitz with husband and son in 1942.
- Famine help: Baron Lionel de Rothschild negotiated an £8 million Famine Loan waiving commission; August Belmont's appeal; Shearith Israel Synagogue, New York raised funds.
- 1938: Chief Rabbi Isaac Herzog asked de Valera to admit six or seven Jewish refugee doctors and dentists - refused.
- Gerald Goldberg: pictured in the South Terrace synagogue, Cork.

OTHER QUOTES AND SYMBOLS
- Rabbi Julia Neuberger (Reform): the future of Jewish life must be about 'vitality, life, buzz', new ways of expressing Jewishness, social service, tolerance - 'let a thousand flowers bloom'.
- Hans Kung: Abraham is the ancestor of Isaac and Jacob (Israel and Jesus) and Ishmael (the Arabs and Muslims) - he has 'tremendous ecumenical significance' for the three Semitic religions.
- Jews are 'God's Chosen People' with a special duty to live God's Law; the Ten Commandments (Decalogue) are shared by Christians and Muslims.
- Menorah: seven-branched candlestick, symbol of Jewish identity, on the Israeli coat of arms with two olive branches. Shalom = peace.

KEY TERMS
- Monotheistic faith, Torah, Covenant, Yahweh, Sabbath, Passover, Yom Kippur, Seder, Holocaust, Tallith, Tefillin, Bar Mitzvah, Bat Mitzvah.

rows.prompt: Give three reasons why Judaism is described as a remarkable faith.
rows.model_answer: It was the first great religion to say there is only one God. It is the 'parent' of Christianity and Islam. Its Ten Commandments, the centre of the Torah, have become the foundation of many of the world's legal codes.

rows.prompt: What is the Covenant, and with whom was it made and renewed?
rows.model_answer: The Covenant is a relationship of total commitment between God and the Jewish people, an experience of God's grace and demands. It was first made through Abraham, renewed by Isaac and Jacob, and by Moses after about four hundred years of slavery in Egypt. It was reaffirmed at Mount Sinai and renewed through the Prophets.

rows.prompt: Explain what Rabbi Jakobovits means by 'deed, not creed'.
rows.model_answer: He means Judaism is mainly a social religion where salvation is collective, not individual. Pure faith means nothing unless it is lived out in behaviour, and Jews are accountable to God. That is why all of Jewish life, from worship to business to diet, is governed by laws.

rows.prompt: Describe the role of the rabbi in the Jewish community.
rows.model_answer: The rabbi leads the local synagogue and is elected by the congregation, to whom he is accountable. His authority is based on learning and study, not on mediating God's love and forgiveness. He is highly respected and may speak for the community when asked, but that is the limit of his authority.

rows.prompt: Why is the Sabbath important to Jews?
rows.model_answer: The Sabbath focuses on God the creator, who rested on the seventh day, and is a memorial of creation and a reminder of total dependence on God. Resting from work, sharing the Sabbath meal and praying together build family and community identity. It is a time to thank God for blessings with joy.

rows.prompt: Describe the Seder meal at Passover.
rows.model_answer: The Seder is a special meal in the home during Passover, which celebrates the deliverance of the Jews from Egypt. The Haggadah, the story of the Exodus, is read, and children play an active part, asking why this night is different. Symbolic foods are eaten, the most important being matzah, unleavened bread.

rows.prompt: Explain Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah.
rows.model_answer: At thirteen a boy becomes Bar Mitzvah, a son of the law. He can be counted in the Minyan, read from the Torah, wears tefillin, fasts on Yom Kippur and is responsible for his actions. At twelve a girl becomes Bat Mitzvah, daughter of the commandment, and must keep the commandments, though she does not lead services in Orthodox synagogues.

rows.prompt: Briefly outline the history of the Jewish community in Ireland.
rows.model_answer: The first reference is in the Annals of Inishfallen in 1079, when five Jews came and were sent back. Sephardic Jews from Spain and Portugal came after the late 15th-century expulsions, and many came from Eastern Europe in the late 19th century, settling in Dublin's 'Little Jerusalem' around Portobello. The population peaked at 5,400 in 1945 and is under 1,200 today.

rows.prompt: Outline the vision of salvation proposed by Judaism.
rows.model_answer: For Jews the central value is reverence for the holiness of all life. Humans are made in God's image, so all life is sacred, and every area, from the exalted to the mundane, has value. Jewish laws therefore cover work, eating, dressing, relationships and nature, and there is no division between religious and secular. Separating the spiritual journey from daily tasks is contrary to Jewish thought. Speculation about the afterlife is of little importance; God will judge how one lives here and now. Wisdom 3 says 'the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God' and 'their hope is full of immortality'. Life after death has been a fundamental belief for two thousand years, though many see the scriptures as symbolic and trust in God's mercy. Yahweh is the God of the Covenant, made with Abraham, reaffirmed at Sinai and renewed through the Prophets. God is merciful, and through Teshuvah, repentance, sinners can return, especially on the Day of Atonement. Rabbi Jakobovits says salvation is collective, never individual, and 'the emphasis is on deed, not creed'. Jews are free to accept or reject the Mitzvot; responding with obedient love accepts God's offer of salvation and brings deep joy.

rows.prompt: Describe the Jewish celebration of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and explain the beliefs they express.
rows.model_answer: Rosh Hashanah means 'head of the year' and is also called the Day of Blowing. It celebrates the birth of the world and the annual judgement of mankind, and is a time of prayer and reflection. An apple dipped in honey is eaten to symbolise a sweet year ahead, and people greet each other with 'May you be written for a good year ahead'. A shofar, a ram's horn, is blown in the synagogue to call people back to the ways of God. This is followed by the Ten Days of Penitence, a time of self-examination with prayers for forgiveness. It ends with Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, a twenty-four-hour fast with services all day and public confession of sin. White robes are worn as a symbol of purity and of the grave. These festivals are purely religious with no historical meaning. They express the belief that God is creator and judge, but also merciful: through Teshuvah, repentance, people can regret their sins, commit never to repeat them and return to God.

rows.prompt: Describe the Jewish rituals surrounding death and mourning.
rows.model_answer: When a Jew dies, close family must arrange the funeral, often helped by the Chevra Kadisha, a 'holy group' of volunteers. Burial usually takes place within twenty-four hours, and in this time close family are called Onen. After burial there are seven days of intense mourning called Shiva. Mourners stay at home together, sit on low stools, cover mirrors and wear a garment torn at the funeral. Appearance does not matter, and neighbours bring food. A candle burns all week and prayers, including the Kaddish, are held in the house. The Kaddish is recited for nearly a year at daily services. Sheloshim, the first thirty days, eases the family back into daily life and ends mourning for a sibling, spouse or child; for a parent, Avelut lasts a whole year. A gravestone is erected after a year. On each anniversary a candle is lit, Kaddish recited, and mourners avoid major celebrations.

rows.prompt: Discuss the challenges facing Judaism in the contemporary world.
rows.model_answer: The history of Judaism is linked to the state of Israel, established in 1948 and known as the Promised Land, where Jews can live their faith without fear of persecution. David Ben Gurion, Israel's first prime minister, said the suffering of Jews in the Diaspora drove immigration, but it was the 'Messianic vision' that led to the State, and the ingathering of exiles is the beginning of its realisation. However, Jews disagree over how much land to claim - all that was promised to Abraham, or less for peace - causing rifts between Zionist zeal and those willing to negotiate. Relations with Islam remain strained because of Middle East tensions, despite a shared monotheism. Another challenge is the rise of secular Jews whose link is identity rather than faith. At the other extreme are ultra-Orthodox Hasidic Jews, largely in Jerusalem, who speak Yiddish and wear distinctive dress. Non-Orthodox Jews - Conservative, Liberal, Progressive and Reform - differ on diet, scripture and women's roles. Keeping a common identity across this range is hard with only about 18 million Jews, 40 per cent in the USA and 20 per cent in Israel. Dialogue with Christians after centuries of anti-Semitism is also an ongoing challenge.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: Israel 1948; Ben Gurion and Messianic vision; land disagreements and Zionism; Jewish-Muslim tension; secular Jews; Hasidic Jews; Conservative/Liberal/Reform; 18 million worldwide; Jewish-Christian dialogue.

rows.prompt: Outline the links between Christianity and Judaism and the steps taken towards reconciliation.
rows.model_answer: Jews and Christians share the Hebrew Bible or Old Testament, and so believe in a common creator and the dignity of all people made in God's image. Judaism's greatest gift to Christianity is Jesus himself; to understand Jesus, Christians must appreciate his Jewishness. Both faiths see love of God and neighbour as inseparable and stress the holiness of creation. Most of the first Christians were Jewish, and their worship, prayer and organisation became the foundation of Church practice. Both treasure the psalms and prophets, and fixed daily prayer times have Jewish roots. Christians use Hebrew words such as Messiah, Amen and Alleluia. However, centuries of anti-Semitism, often encouraged or ignored by the Church, left deep hurt. The Council of Christians and Jews has fostered dialogue. Pope Pius XI said 'We are all spiritually Semites', Pope John XXIII greeted Jews with 'I am Joseph, your brother', and Pope John Paul II called Jews 'our beloved elder brothers' and asked forgiveness, saying at Yad Vashem in 2000 that we remember so that 'never again will evil prevail'. The Sisters of Sion also work for reconciliation.
